title: Alcohol and Depression: How Drinking Affects Your Mood
excerpt: How alcohol and depression feed each other: what drinking does to the brain chemistry behind mood, whether alcohol causes depression, antidepressant risks, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Does alcohol cause depression? How drinking affects mood and brain chemistry, why it backfires when you're low, antidepressant risks, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
> **If you're struggling right now.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **If you are having thoughts of suicide or self-harm, call or text 988** to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US), or call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room. In the UK and Ireland you can call Samaritans on 116 123, any time. Alcohol lowers inhibitions and can make dark thoughts feel more urgent, so if you've been drinking and feel unsafe, put the drink down, move away from anything you could use to hurt yourself, and call someone now.
>
> **See a doctor soon if** you've felt down, empty, or hopeless most days for two weeks or more; you've lost interest in things you usually enjoy; your sleep, appetite, or energy has changed a lot; you're drinking more to get through the day; or you're on an antidepressant and unsure whether alcohol is safe with it. **Get medical care quickly if** you drink heavily most days and notice shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or seeing or hearing things when you stop, because stopping suddenly after long, heavy use can be dangerous and is safest with a doctor's help.

**The honest answer first:** alcohol and depression feed each other. Alcohol is a depressant drug, and while a drink can lift your mood for an hour, regular or heavy drinking tends to make low mood, poor sleep, and anxiety worse over the following days and weeks. People who feel depressed are also more likely to drink to cope, which can turn a rough patch into a loop that's hard to see from the inside. The good news is that the link runs both ways: for many people, cutting back makes a noticeable difference to mood within a few weeks. This guide explains how alcohol affects the brain chemistry behind mood, what the research says about cause and effect, how to tell whether drinking is part of the picture for you, and when to get help.

**The quick rules:** Don't use alcohol as a treatment for low mood; the relief is short and the rebound is real. If you're taking an antidepressant, check with your doctor or pharmacist about alcohol, because some combinations are risky. If you've felt down most days for two weeks or more, talk to a doctor, and be honest about how much you drink so they can help you sort out what's causing what. And if you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, especially while drinking, reach out right away.

## Why Alcohol Is Called a Depressant (and Why That Matters for Mood)

The word "depressant" in pharmacology doesn't mean "makes you sad." It means a drug that slows down the central nervous system, your brain and spinal cord. That's why alcohol makes reactions slower, speech looser, and balance worse. We cover the full science in our guide to [whether alcohol is a depressant](/never-hungover/is-alcohol-a-depressant).

Still, the two meanings are connected. The same brain systems alcohol slows down are the ones that help regulate mood, motivation, and stress. Here's what happens in plain terms.

### It turns up the brain's brake pedal

Alcohol boosts the effect of **GABA**, the main calming chemical messenger in the brain. That's where the early feeling of relaxation comes from. It also blocks **glutamate**, the main "go" signal. More brake and less gas is why a couple of drinks can take the edge off a stressful day.

### It gives a short dopamine and endorphin lift

Drinking triggers a release of dopamine (the chemical tied to reward and motivation) and the body's own feel-good opioids. That lift is a big part of why the first drink feels good. It doesn't last, and the brain doesn't stay neutral afterward.

### The brain pushes back

Your brain is always trying to keep things balanced. When alcohol presses the brake and releases a burst of reward chemicals, the brain responds by turning down its own calming systems and turning up its stress and alertness systems. When the alcohol wears off, you're left with that counter-adjustment and nothing to cancel it out. The result is the familiar next-day mix of jitteriness, irritability, flatness, and low mood. If you mostly notice anxiety and dread the morning after, our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers that specific experience in detail.

With regular drinking, this push-back doesn't fully reset between sessions. The brain's reward system gets less responsive, stress hormones like cortisol stay higher, and everyday pleasures start to feel duller. Many researchers think this is one of the main routes by which steady drinking wears down mood over time.

## Does Alcohol Cause Depression?

This is the question most people searching "depression and drinking alcohol" want answered. The honest answer is that it can contribute, it can mimic depression, and it often makes existing depression worse, but it isn't the only cause and the relationship runs in both directions.

### What the research shows

Large population studies have consistently found that alcohol problems and depression show up together far more often than chance would predict. People with alcohol use disorder are much more likely to have depression, and people with depression are more likely to have drinking problems.

The harder question is which comes first. A widely cited review by Boden and Fergusson, published in the journal *Addiction* in 2011, looked at the evidence and concluded that it was most consistent with a causal link in which alcohol problems increase the risk of depression, rather than only the other way around. That doesn't mean depression never drives drinking. It clearly does for many people. But it does mean that heavy drinking isn't just a side effect of feeling low. It's often part of what keeps the low going.

### Alcohol-induced depression versus depression on its own

Doctors recognize a condition called **substance-induced depressive disorder**, which is listed in the DSM-5, the standard US diagnostic manual. It describes depression that's caused by a substance (alcohol included) rather than existing independently. The symptoms can look exactly the same: sadness, hopelessness, poor sleep, low energy, trouble concentrating.

The key difference is what happens when the drinking stops. In alcohol-induced depression, mood usually improves within a few weeks of not drinking. In independent depression, the symptoms persist even after the alcohol is out of the picture. That's why many clinicians prefer to reassess mood after a stretch of several weeks without heavy drinking before deciding on long-term treatment. It's not a hard rule, and nobody should be told to "wait it out" if they're in real distress, but it's a useful way to untangle the two.

### The short-term dip versus the long-term pattern

There are really two effects worth separating:

- **The next-day dip.** After a night of drinking, low mood, guilt, anxiety, and irritability are common, even in people who don't have depression. This usually fades within a day or two as your brain chemistry, blood sugar, hydration, and sleep recover.
- **The cumulative effect.** Drinking regularly, especially heavily, can wear mood down over weeks and months through poor sleep, disrupted brain chemistry, strained relationships, money stress, and less time for things that protect mood, like exercise and seeing friends.

Most social drinkers only ever deal with the first. But if the dips are getting deeper, lasting longer, or the gaps between them are shrinking, that's worth paying attention to.

## Drinking When You're Depressed: Why It Backfires

When you feel low, a drink can seem like a reasonable way to switch off for the evening. It works, briefly. Here's why it tends to make things worse over the following days.

### The relief is front-loaded, the cost comes later

The calm and lift from alcohol peak while your blood alcohol level is rising. As it falls, the brain's counter-adjustment kicks in. So you trade an hour or two of relief for a longer stretch of feeling worse, often the next morning when you have to function. If you're already depressed, you're starting that rebound from a lower baseline.

### It wrecks the sleep that mood depends on

Sleep and mood are tightly linked, and poor sleep is both a symptom of depression and a risk factor for it. Alcohol helps you fall asleep faster, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night and suppresses REM sleep, the stage tied to emotional processing and memory. You can sleep eight hours after drinking and still wake up unrested. Our guides on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) and [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) go deeper on this.

### It lowers the guardrails

Alcohol reduces inhibitions and impairs judgment. For someone who is depressed, that can mean saying things they regret, making impulsive decisions, or acting on thoughts they'd normally be able to set aside. Public health agencies, including the CDC, have long noted that alcohol is involved in a meaningful share of suicides and suicide attempts. This is the single most important reason not to drink when you're in a very dark place. If that's where you are right now, please use the crisis numbers at the top of this page.

### It pushes aside things that actually help

Time spent drinking or recovering from drinking is time not spent sleeping well, moving your body, seeing people, or doing things that give you a sense of progress. These are the unglamorous basics that research supports for mood. Alcohol doesn't just add a rebound; it crowds out the things that would help you climb out.

### It can blunt treatment

If you're in therapy or taking an antidepressant, regular drinking can make it harder to tell whether treatment is working, and heavy drinking can undercut it. Many doctors will tell you that it's hard to judge an antidepressant fairly while drinking heavily, because alcohol's own effect on mood muddies the picture.

## Alcohol and Antidepressants

If you take an antidepressant, alcohol deserves a specific conversation with your doctor or pharmacist. The risks depend on the drug.

- **SSRIs and SNRIs** (such as sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, and venlafaxine) don't usually cause a dangerous reaction with a single drink, but alcohol can add to drowsiness and dizziness, can worsen the depression and anxiety the medicine is treating, and labels generally advise avoiding it. See our pages on [Zoloft and alcohol](/never-hungover/zoloft-and-alcohol), [Lexapro and alcohol](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol), and [Prozac and alcohol](/never-hungover/prozac-and-alcohol).
- **Bupropion (Wellbutrin)** can lower the seizure threshold, and both heavy drinking and suddenly stopping heavy drinking can raise seizure risk. The prescribing information specifically addresses alcohol. Our [Wellbutrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/wellbutrin-and-alcohol) page explains why.
- **Tricyclics and mirtazapine** tend to be sedating, and alcohol can stack on that sedation, affecting coordination, driving, and breathing at higher amounts.
- **MAOIs** (an older class) can react dangerously with tyramine, which is found in some tap beers, some wines, and aged foods. People on MAOIs get specific diet and drink instructions from their prescriber.

Never stop or skip an antidepressant so that you can drink. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal-like symptoms and can let depression return. For the broader picture across drug classes, see our full guide to [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol). Your doctor or pharmacist can give you advice that fits your exact medicine and dose.

## Is It Depression, a Hangover, or Both?

It can be genuinely hard to tell, especially if you drink most weekends. A few questions can help you sort it out.

**When does the low mood show up?** If it appears the morning after drinking and lifts by midweek, it's probably mostly the rebound. If it's there most days regardless of whether you've been drinking, it's more likely something that needs its own attention.

**How long does it last?** Doctors usually look for symptoms that have been present most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks before diagnosing major depression. A one-day post-drinking slump doesn't meet that bar. Weeks of feeling flat does.

**Do you still enjoy things?** Losing interest or pleasure in activities you normally like is one of the two core symptoms of depression. Two simple screening questions many doctors use (from a short questionnaire called the PHQ-2) ask how often, over the past two weeks, you've had little interest or pleasure in doing things, and how often you've felt down, depressed, or hopeless. If the answer to either is "more than half the days," it's worth talking to a professional.

**What happens when you take a break?** A practical test is to go two to four weeks without drinking, or drinking much less, and track your mood, sleep, and energy. If things clearly improve, alcohol was likely a big part of the picture. If they don't, that's useful information too, and a good reason to see a doctor. If you drink heavily every day, don't stop suddenly on your own; talk to a doctor first (more on that below).

## How Much Drinking Is Linked to Worse Mood?

There's no single safe threshold for mood, and people vary a lot. But the risk clearly rises with heavier and more frequent drinking. Some useful reference points:

- **US Dietary Guidelines:** if adults drink, limit it to 2 drinks or fewer in a day for men and 1 drink or fewer in a day for women.
- **NIAAA's definition of binge drinking:** a pattern that brings blood alcohol to 0.08%, which typically means about 5 or more drinks for men or 4 or more for women in about two hours.
- **NIAAA's definition of heavy drinking:** more than 4 drinks on any day or more than 14 a week for men; more than 3 on any day or more than 7 a week for women.
- **UK low-risk guidance:** no more than 14 units a week, spread over three or more days, with some drink-free days.

A "standard drink" in the US is about 14 grams of pure alcohol: roughly 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits. Many home pours and craft beers are bigger than that, so it's easy to undercount.

The pattern matters as much as the total. Binge sessions produce sharper rebounds, worse sleep, and bigger next-day mood dips than the same amount spread across a week. And drinking alone, drinking specifically to change how you feel, or needing a drink to unwind every night are all signs that alcohol has taken on a mood-management job it isn't good at.

## Who Is More Vulnerable

Some people seem to feel alcohol's mood effects more strongly. You may want to be extra careful if any of these apply:

- **You have a personal or family history of depression or anxiety.** A tendency toward low mood gives the rebound more to work with.
- **You're going through a stressful period**, such as a breakup, job loss, grief, or a big move. This is when drinking to cope is most tempting and most likely to backfire.
- **You're young.** Teen and young-adult brains are still developing, and heavy drinking during these years is linked with a range of mental-health problems later.
- **You sleep poorly already.** If your sleep is fragile, alcohol's sleep disruption hits harder.
- **You take medicines that affect the brain**, including antidepressants, anti-anxiety drugs, sleeping pills, or opioid painkillers. Mixing sedatives with alcohol carries real safety risks.
- **It's winter.** Shorter days already pull mood down for some people, and the holiday season often brings more drinking at the same time.

## A Note on Anxiety

Depression and anxiety often travel together, and alcohol affects both in a similar way: relief in the moment, rebound afterward. Many people who drink to calm social nerves find that their baseline anxiety creeps up over time. If anxiety is more your experience than low mood, our guide on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) covers that side of the loop.

## Practical Steps If You Want to See Whether Alcohol Is Affecting Your Mood

None of this requires a dramatic decision. Small, honest experiments tell you a lot.

1. **Track for two weeks.** Each evening, jot down how many drinks you had and rate your mood, sleep, and energy from 1 to 10. Patterns often jump out faster than you'd expect.
2. **Try a reset.** Take two to four weeks off, or cut back sharply, and keep tracking. Many people notice better sleep within the first week and steadier mood within a few weeks. (Again: if you drink heavily every day, talk to a doctor before stopping.)
3. **Set simple limits when you do drink.** Decide your number before you start, alternate each drink with water, eat a proper meal, and finish drinking a few hours before bed so your sleep has a chance to recover.
4. **Avoid drinking to fix a feeling.** If you notice the urge to drink because you're sad, lonely, or stressed, try a short delay: a walk, a shower, a call to a friend, or 20 minutes of something absorbing. The urge often passes.
5. **Protect the basics.** Regular sleep and wake times, daylight in the morning, some movement most days, and time with people are all supported by research as good for mood. They're also the first things heavy drinking erodes.
6. **Tell your doctor the real numbers.** Doctors hear about drinking all the time and won't be shocked. An accurate picture helps them tell the difference between alcohol-related low mood and depression that needs its own treatment.

## When Drinking Itself Has Become a Health Risk

Most readers of this site are social drinkers, and for them the advice above is enough. But some signs mean alcohol has become a medical issue in its own right, and it's important to say so plainly:

- **Withdrawal symptoms when you stop**, such as shaking hands, sweating, nausea, a racing heart, anxiety, or trouble sleeping that eases when you drink again. In people who have been drinking heavily every day for a long time, stopping suddenly can cause seizures or a dangerous state called delirium tremens, with confusion, fever, and hallucinations. **This is a medical emergency; call 911.** If you drink heavily every day and want to stop, do it with a doctor's help rather than alone.
- **Needing alcohol to start or get through the day.**
- **Being unable to stick to limits you set**, or drinking much more than you meant to, again and again.

If any of these sound familiar, start with your primary care doctor. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) is free, confidential, and open 24 hours a day, and can point you toward local options. Getting help is a normal medical step, not a judgment on you.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol is a depressant in both senses that matter: it slows the brain, and for many people it drags mood down after the initial lift fades. The research supports a two-way relationship, with heavy drinking raising the risk of depression and depression making heavy drinking more likely. Alcohol-related low mood often improves within weeks of cutting back, which makes a break a useful and low-risk experiment. If low mood lasts two weeks or more, if you're on an antidepressant, or if drinking has started to feel necessary, talk to a doctor. And if you ever feel unsafe, call or text 988 (US) or 911 right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol cause depression?**

It can contribute to it and often makes it worse. Large studies show alcohol problems and depression frequently occur together, and a major 2011 review in the journal *Addiction* concluded the evidence was most consistent with alcohol problems increasing the risk of depression. Depression can also lead people to drink more. Alcohol-related low mood often improves within a few weeks of stopping or cutting back.

**Is it okay to drink if I'm depressed?**

It's generally not a good idea. Alcohol gives brief relief, then a rebound that can deepen low mood, worsen sleep, and raise anxiety. It also lowers inhibitions, which can be dangerous if you're having dark thoughts. If you're depressed, talk to a doctor about whether any alcohol is wise for you, especially if you take medication.

**Can drinking make depression worse the next day?**

Yes. As alcohol wears off, the brain overcorrects for its calming effect, and poor sleep, dehydration, and low blood sugar add to it. Many people feel flat, anxious, or guilty the day after drinking. In people who are already depressed, this dip can feel especially heavy. It usually eases within a day or two.

**How long after quitting alcohol does depression improve?**

It varies, but when low mood is mainly caused by drinking, many people notice improvement within a few weeks of stopping or cutting back, often starting with better sleep. If depression persists after about a month without heavy drinking, it may be independent depression that needs its own treatment. If you drink heavily every day, talk to a doctor before stopping.

**Can I drink alcohol on antidepressants?**

It depends on the medicine. Most labels advise avoiding alcohol. With SSRIs, alcohol mainly adds drowsiness and can worsen the depression being treated. Bupropion carries a seizure-related alcohol warning, and MAOIs can react dangerously with tyramine in some drinks. Ask your doctor or pharmacist about your specific medicine and never skip doses to drink.

**How do I know if my drinking is affecting my mood?**

Track your drinks, mood, and sleep for two weeks, then try two to four weeks without alcohol or with much less. If your sleep and mood clearly improve, alcohol was likely part of the problem. Low mood that only shows up after drinking and lifts within a couple of days is probably a rebound, not depression.
